name: Furnas suture technique
lead: The Furnas suture technique is an otoplasty (ear surgery) method that sets back a prominent ear by placing permanent or long-lasting sutures between the conchal cartilage (the bowl of the ear) and the mastoid periosteum behind the ear. It was described by David Furnas in 1968 and is often paired with the Mustardé technique, which forms the antihelical fold with mattress sutures.[1][3]

It addresses ears whose prominence comes mainly from a deep or wide concha. Because it leaves the cartilage uncut, it belongs to the group of cartilage-sparing otoplasty methods.[1][3] In looksmaxxing discussions it is classed as a surgical (hardmaxx) option for the ears.

Published work consists of surgical technique papers and case series. A 2025 overview describes the preparation, surgical steps, postoperative care and complications of Mustardé and Furnas otoplasty,[3] and other surgeons report that these suture methods can recur because of cartilage memory and suture fatigue.[4]
infobox: Typically local or general, per surgeon and patient age

paras: In the Furnas approach, sutures anchor the back of the concha to the mastoid fascia or periosteum, reducing the angle between the ear and the head (the cephaloauricular angle).[1][2] Wikipedia lists it among the suture-only techniques in which the cartilage stays intact, and describes the underlying problem as a deep or wide concha, an underdeveloped antihelical fold, or a protruding lobule.[1]
Surgeons commonly combine it with Mustardé sutures, which recreate the antihelix, so that both the fold and the conchal depth are addressed in one operation.[2][3]

Edward Talbott Ely performed an early elective ear pinback in 1881, and Dieffenbach had described suturing the ear to the mastoid periosteum in 1845.[1] Furnas published conchomastoid suturing in 1968, following Mustardé's and Stenström's methods of 1963.[1][2]
Wikipedia notes that more than 170 otoplasty procedures have been developed.[1]

Reported drawbacks of suture-only methods include recurrence of the deformity through cartilage memory and suture fatigue, and suture extrusion.[4][5] Surgeons have described adding a postauricular dermal flap, either laterally or medially based, to reduce suture extrusion and recurrence.[4][5] Grokipedia gives recurrence of prominence at 3 to 10 percent across otoplasty generally and suture extrusion around 2.5 percent, though its citations are not all specific to this technique.[2]
Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection among otoplasty complications, with suture extrusion the most common.[1]

Evidence is mostly retrospective surgical series. One report of 17 children with prominent lobules combined antitragicus muscle resection and helical tail setback with a Mustardé or Furnas suture technique.[6] A paper presenting a laterally based postauricular dermal flap with Mustardé and Furnas otoplasties reports long-term results aimed at preventing suture extrusion and recurrence.[5] A medially based perichondrio-adipo-dermal flap has been described for the same purpose.[4] A 2025 review in Facial Plastic Surgery summarizes technique and complications.[3] No randomized trials are listed among the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Concha-to-mastoid stitches that pin back a deep ear bowl; an established surgical technique with case-series evidence and a known recurrence risk.
card.note: Suture extrusion and recurrence are reported; surgeon-performed only.

quick.overview:
The Furnas technique is an ear-pinning method that sutures the concha to the bone-covering tissue behind the ear to bring a protruding ear closer to the head. It leaves the cartilage uncut and is often combined with Mustardé sutures.

It is a long-established otoplasty approach documented in surgical case series, mainly for prominent ears in children and adults.
quick.mechanism: Stitches anchor the back of the conchal bowl to the mastoid periosteum, reducing the ear-to-head angle without cutting cartilage.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, overcorrection and recurrence from suture fatigue or cartilage memory. Surgeons have described flaps to reduce extrusion and recurrence.
